questions.stem: The central argument of the passage is that:
options: Confidence and competence are the same thing.
Doubt, far from being a weakness, is the disposition that actually drives the growth of knowledge.
Certainty is always a sign of a well-educated mind.
One should doubt absolutely everything and act on nothing.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: We are trained, almost from infancy, to admire certainty and to be uneasy in the presence of the person who says, plainly, 'I do not know.' Confidence is mistaken for competence, and hesitation for weakness. Yet the history of thought suggests very nearly the opposite. The dogmatist, secure in his conclusions, has no reason to inquire further; having arrived, he stops. It is the doubter — the one willing to hold even his firmest convictions loosely — who keeps looking, and so keeps finding. Doubt, properly understood, is not the enemy of knowledge but its most faithful servant. It is the small, nagging suspicion that the accepted answer might be incomplete which has driven every genuine advance, from the overturning of ancient astronomy to the humblest correction of a household error. This is not to recommend a paralysing scepticism that doubts everything and therefore does nothing; that is merely dogmatism turned inside out. What is wanted is the harder discipline of proportioned belief — holding each conviction exactly as firmly as the evidence warrants, and no more. The truly educated mind is not the one crammed with the greatest number of certainties, but the one that has learned, in the face of a difficult question, to bear the discomfort of not yet knowing.

questions.stem: The 'curious feature of ideas' that opens the passage is that:
options: ideas can be bought and sold like umbrellas.
ideas are worth less than physical property.
ideas cannot be shared between two people.
unlike physical goods, an idea can be given away and still fully kept, and can multiply in the sharing.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: A curious feature of ideas is that they disobey the ordinary laws of property. If I give you my umbrella, I no longer have it; but if I give you my idea, we both possess it entire, and between us it may breed a dozen more. This simple asymmetry explains much about why human progress has clustered so stubbornly in cities. A city is, above all, a device for multiplying the chance encounters out of which new ideas are struck — the overheard remark, the argument in a coffee-house, the rival glimpsed at work and quietly bettered. Density does for thought what a crowded market does for trade. The lone genius, toiling in isolation, is a romantic fiction; in practice, the isolated thinker is starved of exactly the friction and correction that a crowd of peers supplies. It is no accident that the great flowerings of art and science — classical Athens, Renaissance Florence, the coffee-house culture of the Enlightenment — occurred in places where clever people were packed close enough to irritate and inspire one another in roughly equal measure. Where minds are crowded together, the collisions are more frequent, and it is from such collisions, far more than from solitary reflection, that the genuinely new tends to emerge.
